item.title: Opening-up fuels trade in services
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
Opening-up fuels trade in services Wider access to expanding sector expected to bring more opportunities China's deeper opening-up in the services sector is set to bolster the global competitiveness of Chinese service providers and generate new growth opportunities for the global business community, according to market analysts and business executives. Rather than merely aiming to narrow its services trade deficit, China is poised to expand room for both imports and exports via wider market access and regulatory liberalization. Digital services, technology-intensive services and other emerging segments are expected to emerge as key drivers of services trade growth, experts noted. The comments came ahead of the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services, scheduled to run from Wednesday to Sunday in Beijing. Around 90 countries, regions and international organizations will stage exhibitions or events, while more than 1,800 companies will participate off-line, underscoring the fair's role as a key platform for opening up China's services sector and for international cooperation. Unlike trade in goods, services trade involves cross-border transactions in activities ranging from transportation and tourism to telecommunications, computing, education and professional services. In a congratulatory letter to the 2025 China International Fair for Trade in Services, held in Beijing last year, President Xi Jinping said China will remain firmly committed to expanding high-standard opening-up and accelerate the opening of its services market in an orderly manner on platforms including pilot free trade zones and national demonstration zones for the innovative development of trade in services. China is ready to work with all parties to jointly promote open and innovative cooperation in global trade in services, build an open world economy, and continuously inject new impetus into building a community with a shared future for humanity, Xi said. China's trade in services totaled nearly 4.45 trillion yuan ($663 billion) in the first seven months of 2026, up 8.3 percent year-on-year, data from the Ministry of Commerce showed. Services exports rose 17.1 percent year-on-year to over 1.77 trillion yuan. Services imports reached 2.67 trillion yuan, up 3.2 percent from a year earlier. The country's services trade deficit stood at 900.25 billion yuan in the first seven months of this year. Analysts and government officials said China's services trade should not be judged solely by the size of its deficit, as shifts in the composition of imports and exports point to a broader structural transformation, while the country's growing demand for high-quality services is creating substantial opportunities for businesses worldwide. Nie Pingxiang, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation in Beijing, said continued demand for imported services reflects greater market openness, while the rapid expansion of knowledge-intensive exports signals China's growing competitiveness in higher-value services. Knowledge-intensive services also remain a pillar of China's services exports. Exports of such services, which include telecommunications, information technology, finance, intellectual property and other business services, rose 12.2 percent year-on-year to 948.28 billion yuan during the January-July period, accounting for 53.5 percent of the country's total services exports, statistics from the Ministry of Commerce showed. Yan Dong, vice-minister of commerce, said China will step up efforts to cultivate new drivers of trade in services during the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period, as shifts in global industrial chains and accelerating digital and green transitions create new opportunities for the sector. Yan said the government will strengthen the international competitiveness of producer services, promote exports in areas such as research and development, design, testing, maintenance and supply-chain logistics, and harness technologies including artificial intelligence and cloud computing to develop new models for trade in services. Beijing, the host city for the CIFTIS, is emerging as a key testing ground for this next phase of services-sector opening-up, with new measures aimed at expanding market access, facilitating cross-border flows and fostering new drivers of trade in services. Speaking at an investment promotion event in Beijing in late August, Yin Li, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and secretary of the CPC Beijing Municipal Committee, said Beijing will expand exchanges in cross-border e-commerce and international trade and make better use of platforms such as the CIFTIS to deepen economic and trade cooperation. Yin said Beijing aims to bring more high-quality products and services to the Chinese market. The Chinese capital has already expanded opening-up in areas including telecommunications and biotechnology, and introduced measures to facilitate cross-border data flows. It also plans to further open up modern service sectors such as the digital economy and healthcare. Specifically, Beijing has extended the application of its negative list for outbound data transfers from the pilot free trade zone to the entire city, covering nine sectors including medical devices. It will also establish a coordinated development zone linked to the China (Beijing) Pilot Free Trade Zone, focusing on healthcare, AI, integrated circuits and commercial space. The continued opening-up of China's services sector is creating new opportunities for global service providers, as the expansion of two-way trade, digitalization and the internationalization of Chinese companies generates greater demand for cross-border logistics and other professional services. Poh-Yian Koh, president for China at United States logistics company FedEx Corp, said China's continued opening-up and the expansion of trade in services are creating more opportunities for multinational companies in the Chinese market. "More resilient and diversified global supply chains, along with the continued growth of digital trade and cross-border e-commerce, are generating new demand for international logistics and connectivity," she said. To capitalize on these opportunities, FedEx's expanded gateway at Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport in Guangdong province will begin operations by the end of this year. Similar expansion is taking shape in other service sectors. Messe Frankfurt plans to run roughly 45 exhibitions in the country in 2027 and move further into high-end manufacturing and technology, with the German trade fair organizer exploring new shows in areas including power electronics, additive manufacturing and factory automation. Stephan Buurma, a board member of Messe Frankfurt, said the company will expand its portfolio through acquisitions and new launches, moving beyond established areas such as textiles, consumer goods and automotive.

item.title: Plan to boost special education nationally
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
Plan to boost special education nationally Focus on building inclusive, accessible system for children with disabilities A new action plan, released by China's Ministry of Education and six other central government departments, has set a target to maintain the 97 percent enrollment rate of school-age children with disabilities in compulsory education through 2030. Released on Aug 31, the plan outlines a comprehensive push to build a high-quality special education system that is inclusive, accessible and convenient, with the goal of enhancing the ability of children with disabilities to integrate into society and pursue lifelong development. China has made historic strides in special education, with the number of special education schools, enrolled students and full-time teachers all increasing significantly since 2012, according to official data. By 2025, the country had 2,464 special education schools, serving 927,000 students and employing 85,100 specialized teachers — up 33 percent, 145 percent and 95 percent, respectively, compared with 2012. However, education authorities cautioned that the rapid expansion has also exposed persistent weaknesses. Insufficient resource allocation, uneven teaching quality, limited digital integration and incomplete support mechanisms remain hurdles to further progress. The plan identifies five key tasks. The first is to expand resources for special education by optimizing educational placement for children with disabilities, improving pathways for further study and fully safeguarding their right to education. The second is to improve education quality by deepening curriculum and teaching reforms, accelerating efforts to improve education for children with autism, strengthening professional support for special education, and integrating vocational education with employment pathways for students with disabilities. Digital transformation is the third priority, with the plan encouraging the use of artificial intelligence to support the development of special education. The fourth task is to strengthen inclusive development by consolidating the funding mechanism for special education, improving school conditions and strengthening the teaching workforce. The fifth is to expand international exchanges and cooperation in special education. The plan also calls for expanding opportunities for students with disabilities to receive education at the high school level and above. It supports the integrated development of secondary vocational and vocational undergraduate education for students with disabilities, and encourages special education secondary vocational schools to collaborate with higher vocational institutions to offer five-year programs. It also supports universities in developing majors suitable for students with disabilities and actively admitting qualified candidates. Universities are required to strengthen academic support, living services and career guidance for students with disabilities. Shandong Medical and Pharmaceutical University has introduced targeted admission policies and a full-chain support system for students with disabilities, said Huang Fei, the university's president. For applicants with visual or hearing impairments, the university participates in a joint entrance examination with four other institutions through a separate admission channel. For applicants with limb disabilities, all undergraduate majors are open to them as long as they meet the national cutoff scores, and they enjoy the same right to change majors as other students, with no additional barriers, Huang told China Central Television. The university also provides integrated services tailored to students' diverse needs, covering academic support, practical training, career placement and further studies, he said. Yu Muyang, a visually impaired undergraduate student majoring in traditional Chinese medicine at the university, had worried about studying diagrams and conducting specimen experiments. But on campus, he found Braille textbooks, tactile anatomical models and dedicated laboratories, as well as a team of special education teachers, psychologists and rehabilitation therapists. Yu said he never feels isolated in public or elective courses, where he studies alongside students without disabilities. The university actively connects students with hospitals and rehabilitation centers for internships and employment, and some senior students have gone on to pursue master's degrees in law. "We experience equal access under adapted conditions, and I believe we can create our own brilliant futures through our abilities," Yu said.

item.title: Global food system faces mounting resilience crisis
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
Global food system faces mounting resilience crisis Experts warn of 'perfect storm' due to disruptions to energy, fertilizer trade Global cereal production is on track for its second-largest harvest on record in 2026, according to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization. Yet, the data also show that world food prices rose in August to their highest since late 2022. The seemingly contradictory figures reveal the global food system's ongoing "resilience crisis", a systemic fragility that persists even when aggregate supply appears adequate. Although there is no widespread systemic food shortage currently, global food security is under significant pressure, driven mainly by high energy prices, extreme weather events and conflicts, experts said. "We are seeing pressure on production, agricultural inputs and trade logistics at the same time," said Maximo Torero, chief economist at the FAO. On the agricultural production front, the frequent extreme weather witnessed this summer and a strengthening El Nino weather pattern are threatening crops worldwide. The UN World Food Programme's early analysis projects that the 2026-27 El Nino could push at least 49 million more people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027. Beyond climate, conflict is placing comprehensive pressure on the food system. According to the World Bank's Commodity Markets Outlook report issued in April, the war in the Middle East has significantly disrupted global commodity markets, with energy prices projected to surge 24 percent this year and fertilizer prices expected to rise about 31 percent. Fertilizer affordability is set to fall to its worst level since 2022, eroding farmer incomes and jeopardizing future crop yields. Zhang Shuai, an associate professor at the School of Government at Shanghai University of Political Science and Law, said conflicts also directly destabilize food production. He cited the Russia-Ukraine conflict as an example, which has left millions of hectares of Ukrainian arable land abandoned and much of its agricultural infrastructure destroyed. Such conflicts also jeopardize food supply security, Zhang added. "Whether it's the Russia-Ukraine conflict or the US-Iran war, both have disrupted global food supply chains by affecting critical international shipping routes. The Ukraine conflict's effect is direct, curtailing grain exports from both nations." A report from JPMorgan, titled Food Security is National Security: A Compounding Storm, warns that global food costs could climb 5 percent in the first half of 2027, suggesting that the next wave of global inflation may not originate at the fuel station but at the grocery shelf. Torero said that compared with previous global food crises, "the 2026 shock is potentially more complex because it simultaneously affects the inputs needed to produce the next crop". "The Strait of Hormuz is not simply another grain-export corridor," he said. "Around 30 percent of global fertilizer trade passes through the strait; the Gulf region accounts for approximately 30 to 35 percent of global urea supply and 50 percent of sulfur. When the crisis escalated, tanker traffic fell by more than 90 percent, and an estimated 3 to 4 million metric tons of fertilizer trade per month were stalled." The implications are profound. "When wheat disappears from one exporter, another producer can eventually plant more wheat," Torero said. "You cannot create new natural gas, ammonia, urea or sulfur production capacity within a planting season. These are capital-intensive industries, so short-term supply elasticity is very low. "That is why the crop calendar matters so much. FAO has warned that if the disruption persists beyond roughly three months, the effect moves from prices into fertilizer application, planting decisions and eventually yields in the following harvests," he added. Long Wenjin, an associate professor at the College of Economics and Management of China Agricultural University, said the true danger lies not just in the combination of energy prices, extreme weather and conflicts, but in their cascading amplification across the entire system. Purchasing power This extends from agricultural inputs and food production to trade, transport, financial markets and fiscal capacity, ultimately affecting household purchasing power, Long said. "This dynamic can rapidly convert localized production shortfalls or shipping disruptions into escalating food prices, fiscal strains and widespread livelihood difficulties." This looming food security crisis differs significantly from previous ones, being "far more systemic, characterized by stronger cross-market linkages, long-term implications, and increasingly politicized dynamics", he said. "With multiple key waterways and related markets simultaneously under pressure, it's coalescing into a perfect storm sweeping across the global agri-food system," he said. Experts noted that the current crisis has exposed structural weaknesses within the global food system, as they anticipate high volatility in global food markets and a continued upward trend in commodity price levels in the coming months. Torero of the FAO highlighted the excessive dependence on choke points. "Black Sea disruption affects cereals; Hormuz affects energy, fertilizers and freight. A localized geopolitical event can therefore propagate throughout the global agri-food system." Another critical weakness is "input dependency", he said. "Food security depends not only on grain stocks but on fertilizer, energy, seeds, water and finance. When those inputs become unavailable or unaffordable, the effect appears in the next harvest." Long said the fundamental vulnerability exposed by this crisis is the global food system's long-standing pursuit of low costs and high efficiency without retaining adequate safety margins or alternative capacities for extreme shocks. To navigate this crisis, experts propose a dual approach focusing on immediate actions and long-term systemic reforms. In the short term, Long said, the priority must be ensuring the smooth flow of food, fertilizer, seeds and other critical agricultural products and inputs. Over the long run, Torero said "the fundamental shift" should be from paying for losses after a crisis to financing prevention before those losses become irreversible. Long echoed the view, saying the crisis response model should shift from single-commodity supply management to integrated food production system governance that coordinates agricultural production, energy, trade, nutrition, finance and social welfare. "Ultimately, the global food crisis can only be resolved by maintaining peace, promoting development, and upholding open cooperation," he said.

item.title: Pinglu Canal set for Sept 16 launch
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
Pinglu Canal set for Sept 16 launch The Pinglu Canal, China's first river-to-sea canal project planned and coordinated at the national level since 1949, will open for shipping on Sept 16, authorities of the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region announced on Monday. The canal, designed for vessels of up to 5,000 metric tons, runs 134.2 kilometers from the Xijiang River to the Beibu Gulf. It has an estimated total investment of 72.7 billion yuan ($10.8 billion). "Once operational, goods from Southwest China shipped via the Pinglu Canal will cut inland shipping distances by more than 560 km compared with traditional outbound routes. Overall logistics costs will drop 18 to 30 percent, saving society more than 5 billion yuan in transport expenses each year and reshaping logistics patterns across Southwest China," said Zhang Zhiwen, deputy secretary-general of the Guangxi regional government and a government spokesperson. The savings will lower corporate operating costs, facilitate domestic and foreign trade, boost household incomes and inject strong momentum into high-quality regional development, Zhang added. The project prioritized public wellbeing throughout construction. More than 70,000 local residents participated in construction work, receiving about 2.6 billion yuan in payments. Alongside the canal, authorities built 17 resettlement communities, reconstructed or newly built six primary schools, adding 1,089 student seats and laid 72,000 meters of water supply pipelines to address drinking water difficulties for tens of thousands of residents. Major civil works have passed official acceptance, while a smart integrated river-sea dispatch platform has been launched online. Real-ship navigation trials and full-scale operational drills have also been completed, with all regulatory permits in place, leaving the canal fully ready for service, Zhang said. Li Hengchang, a member of the Communist Party of China committee and deputy general manager of Pinglu Canal Group, said the new logistics corridor needs growing vessel traffic and cargo volumes to reach its full potential. Guangxi has set tentative lock charges that balance sustainable facility operation with affordable shipping costs. According to Li, commercial vessels transiting the canal's three hubs — Madao, Qishi and Qingnian ship locks — will be exempt from lockage fees from the opening day through Dec 31. Starting Jan 1, 2027, the fee will be 1 yuan per gross ton for each lock passage. The Xinfu and Qinzhou water service zones along the canal offer berthing, provisions, diesel, clean energy and LNG refueling, fresh water supplies, as well as collection services for domestic waste, bilge water and oily wastewater from vessels and crews. Cargo recruitment efforts are well underway, according to Lin Anren, a second-level inspector with the Guangxi Development and Reform Commission. Guangxi has held cargo-matching events in Yunnan, Chongqing and multiple local cities, attracting more than 1,500 participating enterprises, Lin said. Going forward, Guangxi will push ahead with the Pinglu Canal Economic Belt, formulate and execute the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) implementation scheme, and develop port-oriented, water-friendly industries to drive sustained cargo growth along the waterway. "The opening of the Pinglu Canal, the backbone of the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, marks a new starting point rather than an end," Zhang said. In the future, Guangxi will upgrade its water transport network and develop its marine-focused economy. It will seize opportunities under the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and align with key national strategies, including the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area and the Yangtze River Economic Belt. "Using this landmark canal, Guangxi will boost the China-ASEAN community of shared destiny and advance China's new development paradigm goals," Zhang said.

item.title: High-end chip from Huawei released
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
High-end chip from Huawei released First high-performance processor to adopt the company's LogicFolding Huawei Technologies Co on Monday unveiled its latest flagship chip, the Kirin 9050 Pro, marking the company's first new high-performance Kirin processor launch at a flagship event since its Mate 40 smartphones global debut six years ago. The chip, which powers Huawei's newly released Mate XT 2 tri-fold smartphone, is the industry's first high-performance processor to adopt the company's LogicFolding technology. The approach rearranges logic units within a single chip into layered stacks — akin to converting a single-floor layout into a duplex — and adds vertical interconnect channels that function like "elevators" to shorten signal paths and reduce latency. The result is a 42 percent improvement in overall device performance over the previous generation chip, Huawei said. Yu Chengdong, Huawei's executive director and chairman of the terminal business group, described the chip at the Guangzhou, Guangdong province launch event as "super fast, intelligent and cool" — calling it the most powerful Kirin chip to date. The Kirin 9050 Pro delivers substantial improvements in large-file loading, multitasking, rendering performance and on-device artificial intelligence capabilities, Huawei said. According to real-world test data, the chip packs 55 percent more transistors per square millimeter than its predecessor, the Kirin 9030 Pro — jumping from approximately 155 million to 238 million transistors per sq mm in a single generation. The Lingxi CPU delivers a 24 percent increase in single-core peak performance and a 52 percent boost in multi-core concurrent performance. The breakthrough comes from LogicFolding, a concept rooted in what Huawei calls the "Tau Scaling Law" — a theoretical framework first proposed by He Tingbo, president of Huawei's semiconductor business, in May. On Friday, He published her third update in less than four months on the ChinaXiv preprint platform, a paper directly addressing industry skepticism about whether dense 3D stacking would inevitably lead to higher power density and heat. He's answer is a definitive no. The paper explains that the majority of energy consumption in modern chips comes not from computation itself, but from moving data across long on-chip wires — a phenomenon she likens to a worker's daily energy being consumed not by desk work, but by commuting. Logic-Folding replaces long horizontal journeys with short vertical connections — the chip's "elevators" — cutting typical core wiring length by about 20 percent and reducing some critical paths by up to 70 percent. She emphasized that "Tau is a time-scaling law, not an energy-scaling law" — the real value lies in converting saved time into lower voltage and frequency, rather than chasing peak performance at the cost of efficiency. Xiang Ligang, director-general of the Information Consumption Alliance — a telecom industry association, said that for Huawei, the Kirin 9050 Pro represents more than just a performance upgrade — it's a statement that the company's chip design capabilities continue to advance even as its access to US-related advanced chip manufacturing equipment remains constrained. The Kirin 9050 Pro's debut also comes as the global foldable smartphone market reaches a historic inflection point. Counterpoint Research said cumulative global foldable smartphone shipments are expected to surpass 100 million units by the end of 2026 — some eight years after the first commercial foldable device launched in 2019. The research firm projects the market will accelerate to 37 percent year-on-year growth in 2027, driven by Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold8 series and Apple's anticipated entry into the foldable segment.

item.title: 43 dead, 519 missing after mudslide hits border port in Xizang
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
President Xi Jinping urges all-out rescue, relief efforts after mudslide hits border port in Xizang Level-II emergency response activated after mudslide hits border port in Xizang On the morning of Aug 26, a devastating mudslide originating in Nepal caused mass casualties and left hundreds missing at Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region. But why was the ice-rock avalanche that precipitated the mudslide so hard to predict? Why did Gyirong take such a massive hit? And what has made rescue efforts so challenging? In this video, we uncover the full picture by tracing the disaster from the source glacier over 100km downstream to Gyirong Port. Chinese commercial satellites are stepping up monitoring of glaciers upstream from Gyirong Port in the Xizang autonomous region, looking for cracks and surface shifts that could signal further hazards as rescue operations continue following the Aug 26 mudslide. Three Synthetic Aperture Radar, or SAR, satellites operated by Spacety, a commercial aerospace company based in Changsha, Hunan province, are providing updated imagery to the rescue command center in Gyirong county, Shigatse. The satellites have already been used to monitor two barrier lakes and assess damage to National Highway G216 in the disaster-hit area. The latest focus is the glacier area upstream, where the team is using satellite imagery to track changes in the ice surface and identify potential risks, said Jiang Lin, a satellite engineer with the company who is working at the front-line rescue command center. "If we spot a potential risk, the data will be provided to the rescue command center for further ground-based checks," Jiang said. "By combining satellite technology with ground information, we have built a multilayered monitoring system to provide timely and accurate information for rescue operations." The team has also introduced Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar, or InSAR, technology to improve its ability to detect surface deformation. By comparing radar images of the same area taken at different times, the technology can detect ground movement at the millimeter-to-centimeter scale and cover large areas without requiring monitoring equipment to be installed on the ground. SAR technology is particularly useful in Gyirong's mountainous terrain as it can operate at night and penetrate clouds and rain that may obstruct optical satellite observations. "Think of SAR satellites as CT scanners for the Earth," Jiang said. "As the satellite moves along its orbit, it actively transmits microwave signals to create high-resolution images, even in heavy rain or at midnight." Spacety joined the emergency response shortly after the mudslide hit the Gyirong Port area. Within 20 minutes of receiving a request for support, the team adjusted its satellite imaging plans to prioritize the affected area, Jiang said. The first SAR images were obtained in the early hours of Aug 27. Jiang and his colleagues arrived at the rescue command center later that day to coordinate satellite observations with the needs of teams on the ground. Satellite imagery obtained on Aug 27 and Aug 28 identified two barrier lakes, helping rescuers assess potential flooding risks downstream. In SAR images, water surfaces appear dark, while debris and damaged slopes appear brighter, allowing analysts to identify the lakes and assess their extent, Jiang said. The satellites have also captured damaged sections of National Highway G216 near Gyirong Port, providing imagery of road-clearing routes and excavation work. With three satellites passing over the affected area at different times and from different angles, the team can repeatedly update observations of key sites, providing rescuers with a more complete picture of changing conditions. "By working here with the frontline rescue teams, we can understand their needs firsthand and respond as quickly as possible," Jiang said. "We aim to bridge the last mile between space technology and rescue operations." Contact the writers at limuyun@chinadaily.com.cn China on Monday said it had invited foreign journalists to visit the mudslide-hit areas of Gyirong in the Xizang autonomous region to learn about rescue efforts and reconstruction progress in response to the international media's close attention to reporting on the debris flow disaster. The visit came after round-the-clock repair work had initially reopened the roads to the disaster zone, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said at a regular news briefing. China had invited journalists from eight foreign media outlets, including NBC, CNN, Reuters, RT and the Press Trust of India, to enter the hardest-hit areas to learn about rescue and reconstruction progress, Mao said. They also attended a news conference held by the regional government, she added. As reports from these journalists have been released, Mao said, "China will continue to make every effort to carry out search-and-rescue operations and handling of the aftermath, and release the latest information on the disaster and rescue operations in a timely manner." After days of relentless search and rescue efforts, Xiao Fugui, a police officer at the entry-exit border inspection station in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, looked gaunt and exhausted. Despite his weary appearance, he repeatedly insisted that he was not at all tired. "All I want is to find my workmates," he said on Thursday, gripping an iron shovel with determination, his brow furrowed. On Aug 26, a massive mudslide devastated Gyirong Port, a vital land link between China and Nepal. As of 6 pm on Saturday, 993 personal belongings had been recovered while 519 people remain unaccounted for. Xiao was driving toward the port when the disaster struck. "I was just 4 or 5 kilometers away when I saw several cars pulled over," he said. "I got out and asked other drivers what was happening — everyone was panicked, saying the water level had risen sharply near the port." Concerned for their safety, he instructed the two female colleagues in his car to get out and find a safe place, then continued driving alone to assess the situation. Upon realizing it was a mudslide, Xiao immediately alerted authorities. "The muddy water was rushing toward me, so I threw the car into reverse and backed up about 500 meters before stopping," said Xiao in a tense voice. "I was terrified the car would be swept away. What really scared me was not knowing what had happened to my workmates at the port." As visibility dropped sharply and the road ahead was blocked, Xiao found himself trapped. Reflecting on that moment, he said, "I really walked through the gates of hell that day." Driven by worry and a deep sense of duty, Xiao joined the rescue teams. By Sunday, he had reached the vicinity of the port and immediately immersed himself in the relief efforts. "As soon as I arrived, I started moving supplies, then began searching. I found clothing, shoes and crushed vehicles belonging to the missing. Every single item I saw pierced my heart like a needle." Originally from Qinghai province, 39-year-old Xiao has worked in Xizang for 17 years, with 11 of those years at the Gyirong entry-exit border inspection station, primarily handling publicity affairs. "For many years, I've spent almost every day with my workmates — filming their patrols, writing about their lives guarding this border," he said. "This port, these people — they've become part of me." On the first day of the rescue, Xiao and other workers camped in a tent by a reservoir halfway up the mountain near the border port. He did not sleep at all. "The rain was so heavy that night — water poured down the slopes and merged into the river. The sound of rain, rushing water and collapsing hillsides all mixed together. It made my heart sink. I didn't dare to sleep, and I couldn't sleep anyway," he said. As he spoke, he picked up the shovel and resumed digging. "I have only one thought: no matter what, I want to find my workmates. I want to bring them home," he added. Contact the writers at caoyin@chinadaily.com.cn As dawn broke in Gyirong county following another night of continuous rain on Saturday, He Lei, a psychological counselor, began another day of providing counseling services to search and rescue personnel working on the front line of the mudslide-stricken Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region. "Through our work these days, we have found that our soldiers are quite resilient. They are focused on fulfilling their missions here and are fully aware of the significance of helping every family affected by the disaster," said He, a member of the medical and disease prevention team with the logistics support department of the People's Liberation Army Xizang Military Command. As of Thursday, the PLA and the People's Armed Police Force had deployed 726 personnel to support rescue and relief operations following the mudslide, according to official data. Li Guokai, head of the medical and disease prevention team, said the team is responsible for providing medical and psychological services to rescue workers and affected villagers during patrol visits, disinfecting key sites and monitoring health risks. According to He, for those experiencing stress responses such as panic attacks or physical stiffness, the most important thing is to divert their attention from whatever is triggering the reaction. "We have a method called 'look, listen, smell and move.' For instance, we will guide soldiers in need to identify three objects with specific characteristics in their surroundings, then listen for distinct sounds, identify several different smells and engage in a simple physical movement, such as stamping their feet," she said. "This rapid redirection of attention helps alleviate immediate physiological stress responses," she said. In addition to patrolling military bases involved in rescue operations on a daily basis, He also goes to the core area to provide on-site assistance when needed. "As members of the military, we cannot shy away from difficult conditions," she said. "I wanted to be on the front line myself — to see if any soldiers needed support and to teach them techniques they can use on their own to manage stress." Tan Xiangdong, Party chief of the Xizang autonomous regional health commission, said at a news conference on Wednesday that national and regional health authorities had organized three batches of psychological health experts, totaling more than 210. Frontline rescuers have access to psychological risk assessments, group and individual counseling, as well as pocket guides designed to help them understand stress reactions and learn effective ways to cope, Tan said. Contact the writers at wangxiaoyu@chinadaily.com.cn For Hao Zhen, who was among a network of volunteers coordinating relief efforts in disaster-hit Gyirong county, rendering aid can come in many forms. When a devastating mudslide struck Gyirong, a remote border area in the Xizang autonomous region, Hao did not hesitate. While professional rescue teams searched the hardest-hit areas, Hao and his fellow volunteers worked behind the scenes to distribute supplies, meals and arrange accommodation for displaced residents and rescue workers. The 27-year-old was among 17 volunteers from China's Go West program who joined relief efforts in Gyirong township after the Aug 26 disaster. "When the disaster first happened, a lot of affected residents and rescuers arrived in the area all at once," Hao said. "The first thing we had to do was make sure they had somewhere to stay and food to eat." As relief supplies poured in, the volunteers counted, sorted and moved thousands of boxes donated by a number of Red Cross organizations, companies and foundations. They also helped with logistics at the local emergency response headquarters and collected and organized information from the disaster area. The experience gave Hao a new understanding of the mechanics of disaster relief efforts. "Before this, I had only read news stories about volunteers helping after disasters," he said. "Now I realize that you don't have to be on the search-and-rescue front line to make a difference. Keeping things running behind the scenes matters, too." Born in 1999, Hao was the oldest among the volunteers working in Gyirong who came from various parts of the country, including Heilongjiang, Jiangxi and Shandong provinces, as well as Xizang, and have backgrounds ranging from medicine to education. The work brought practical challenges. Only two of the 17 volunteers spoke Tibetan, creating communication difficulties at shelters. Local township officials often stepped in to assist with interpretations. Food and accommodation were also stretched in the first few days, as large numbers of residents, rescuers and support workers arrived in the small border town. Hao said the situation gradually improved as local authorities coordinated with hotels and restaurants to provide additional support. Five other Go West program volunteers remained in the county seat, where they welcomed relatives of missing people, assisted families and handled calls and follow-ups through the 12345 public service hotline. Volunteers from nearby counties, including Lhaze and Dingri, also arrived to help. For Hao, Gyirong is a long way from home — nearly 5,700 kilometers from Shuangyashan in Heilongjiang. He usually makes the journey home once a year. He arrived in Gyirong in February 2025 to join the Go West program and planned to stay for three years. His family initially tried to talk him out of the move, worried about the distance and the physical demands of living at high altitude. "But I thought, if everyone worries about the hardship and the distance, places like this will have fewer and fewer young people willing to come," Hao said. The physical challenges are real. When Hao first arrived in Gyirong, he found that he did not have the same stamina he had at lower elevations. He also experienced heart palpitations when he first joined the relief effort. After more than a year on the plateau, however, he said his body has largely adapted. His family still worries about him, particularly after learning that he was involved in the disaster response. "But the disaster happened right here, where we work and live," Hao said. "Since we chose to come here as volunteers, helping when something like this happens is simply part of what we should do." The Aug 26 mudslide at Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-altitude glacier in Nepal. As of 6 pm on Saturday, 43 people had been confirmed dead and 519 others remained missing, according to the local emergency response and rescue command headquarters. For Hao, the experience has also changed the way he approached the small tasks that fill much of his day. Moving boxes, arranging accommodation and making sure people have meals may be far removed from the dramatic scenes of a search-and-rescue operation, but he no longer sees them as minor jobs. "My biggest hope now is that we can keep the support work running smoothly, that all the rescuers return safely and that there are no more secondary disasters," he said. Contact the writers at luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn China has established communication and information-sharing mechanisms with the 23 home countries of the 261 foreign nationals who remain missing following the mudslide that struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border. Through the China-Nepal disaster information exchange mechanism, meteorological, hydrological, glacial lake and glacier data are being transmitted to Nepal daily, a senior official said on Sunday. Ren Wei, executive deputy commander of the emergency rescue headquarters and executive vice-chairman of the Xizang autonomous region, said all relevant information had been promptly communicated to the respective embassies in China through diplomatic channels. A 24-hour dedicated hotline for families of the missing foreign nationals has also been established and has received 509 calls as of Sunday. Each inquiry had been followed up on, with responses relayed to the next of kin, Ren said. At the request of the Nepali side, the Chinese government dispatched tunnel rescue and DNA identification experts to Nepal, along with emergency relief supplies. The Xizang autonomous regional government also provided 320 metric tons of Bailey bridge components — designed for the rapid assembly of temporary bridges — and other relief supplies to Nepal. Yang Lahong, deputy director of the Xizang foreign affairs office, said the region had carried out verification of information on the missing people in a rigorous, prudent and standardized manner. The region released basic information on the missing people initially identified a day after the disaster. On Aug 30, it published additional details of the missing foreign nationals verified through joint investigations and rapid cross-checking by multiple departments. While the breakdown by country and number of missing people was made public by authorities, the specific list and personal details have not been released due to privacy concerns. Instead, the information was communicated to the relevant embassies through diplomatic channels, with a collective briefing held on Tuesday, Yang said. For safety reasons and to ensure efficient and orderly rescue work, no non-professionals were allowed to enter the affected core areas until conditions were fully prepared, she said. To keep the public informed while ensuring safety, a small number of Chinese journalists were arranged to accompany rescue teams into the core areas despite the difficult terrain. Their reports and footage were subsequently released and widely used by domestic and international media, Yang said. Regarding the families of the missing foreign nationals, the region expressed sympathy during these difficult times. In addition to providing regular authoritative updates and notifying families through diplomatic channels, authorities have kept the 24-hour hotline operating, with personnel diligently verifying information and providing feedback. Currently, efforts are focused on rescue and recovery. After the search operation concludes, authorities will confirm and notify the status of deceased foreign nationals and assist their families with follow-up procedures. For those who remain missing, assistance will be provided within China's legal framework, including arrangements for their families to visit Xizang, in coordination with relevant foreign diplomatic missions, she added. Contact the writers at zoushuo@chinadaily.com.cn Chinese experts have intensified monitoring of landslides, barrier lakes, glaciers and glacial lakes around the mudslide-hit area in Gyirong county, Xizang autonomous region, to guard against secondary disasters and ensure the safety of ongoing rescue operations. The mudslide, which occurred on Aug 26, caused significant casualties and left many people missing in the region. Su Pengcheng, a researcher at the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said during a group interview with Chinese and foreign media in Gyirong on Sunday that experts from multiple government departments and research institutions had been mobilized soon after the disaster. While rescue operations were underway, specialists began analyzing the causes of the disaster and assessing potential geological risks to provide safety support for frontline rescuers, Su said. The road leading to the core rescue area was reopened in less than a week, while monitoring and risk assessment continued in parallel. One priority has been closely tracking changes in a barrier lake formed after the disaster to prevent any sudden discharge from threatening downstream areas. Authorities have also deployed professional monitoring equipment, including remote slope-deformation cameras, slope radars and satellite remote-sensing systems, to continuously assess the stability of slopes and residual deposits in the disaster-hit area. Particular attention has been paid to potentially unstable material remaining on slopes near the affected valley, which could trigger further landslides or debris flows and pose risks to downstream rescue operations, Su said. Experts have also conducted comprehensive geological hazard surveys around five villages in the affected river basin and along National Highway G216, a key emergency rescue route, to identify potential dangers and ensure the route remains safe. Monitoring has extended beyond the core disaster area, with satellite and aerial remote sensing being used to track changes in surrounding glaciers and glacial lakes, which are widely distributed across the high-altitude region. Su said the operation has brought together expertise from emergency management, natural resources, meteorology and water resources authorities, as well as research institutions, with a range of monitoring equipment deployed. Experts are also using real-time images transmitted by drones to assess changing conditions. Their findings are promptly relayed to downstream teams, allowing search and rescue personnel to adjust operations when risks emerge. Su said the coordinated monitoring system is intended to provide continuous early warning of possible secondary geological disasters while rescue work continues. The recent debris flow that occurred on the Nepali side has underscored the urgent need for cross-border cooperation in disaster early warning, said Norbu Tsering, acting mayor of Shigatse, on Sunday. Su Pengcheng, a researcher at the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, Chinese Academy of Sciences, said that source zones of ice-rock avalanches at high altitudes are extremely difficult to access because of cold temperatures, low oxygen levels and rugged terrain. Cross-border river basins also have observational blind spots, while ground equipment can suffer from power and communication problems. Precursor signals are often subtle, and warning windows can be only a matter of minutes — far too short for traditional single-point monitoring to cover entire watersheds, he said. Given that climate change is accelerating such rare but severe events, it is essential to conduct risk assessments of glacier instability, fill upstream monitoring gaps and introduce new geophysical detection technologies for full-chain dynamic monitoring, Su said. He proposed developing a "space-air-ground" noncontact monitoring network to reduce dependence on on-site stations at extreme altitudes. A tiered approach — involving wide-area satellite scanning, targeted high-resolution monitoring and downstream alert systems — could provide valuable additional time for evacuation, he said. Su also called for cross-border scientific collaboration and joint early-warning mechanisms. Since disasters do not respect borders, he called for data exchanges and shared risk assessments with Himalayan nations through existing international platforms. He also urged the creation of rapid notification channels to extend early warnings across entire upstream-downstream basins. Norbu said the Xizang autonomous region has invested heavily in glacial-lake monitoring in recent years. A baseline survey using satellite imagery, fieldwork and glacier data identified more than 33,000 glacial lakes across the region. Authorities have placed 187 high-risk lakes under satellite monitoring, with 49 of those also covered by ground sensors and drone surveillance, he said. A multi-agency data-sharing platform now links meteorological, hydrological, natural resources and emergency departments. Expert panels regularly review glacial-lake risks, and a short-term early-warning system has been activated, along with evacuation drills for downstream communities during the flood season, he said. China has established communication and information-sharing mechanisms with the affected countries as 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries remain missing following a recent mudslide at Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border. Through the China-Nepal disaster information exchange mechanism, meteorological, hydrological, glacial lake, and glacier data are transmitted daily to Nepal, a senior official stated on Sunday. A 24-hour dedicated hotline for families of the missing foreign nationals has been established, receiving 509 calls to date, with each inquiry followed up and responses relayed to the next of kin, Ren added. At Nepal's request, the Chinese government has sent experts in tunnel rescue and DNA identification to Nepal, along with emergency material aid. Additionally, the local government of the Xizang autonomous region has provided 320 metric tons of Bailey bridge components and other relief supplies to Nepal. Yang Lahong, deputy director of the foreign affairs office of the Xizang autonomous region, noted that the region has rigorously and prudently verified the personnel information of the missing individuals. The basic information of the missing persons was initially released the day after the disaster, and further details were published on Aug 30, verified through joint investigations and rapid cross-checking by multiple departments. While the breakdown by country and number has been made public, specific lists and personal details have not been released due to privacy concerns; instead, this information has been communicated to the relevant embassies through diplomatic channels, with a collective briefing held on Sept 1, she said. For safety reasons and to ensure efficient and orderly rescue work, non-professionals were not allowed into the affected core areas until conditions were fully prepared. To keep the public informed while ensuring safety, a small number of Chinese journalists accompanied rescue teams into the core areas, overcoming difficult terrain. Their reports and footage were subsequently released and widely used by domestic and international media, Yang said. Regarding the families of the missing foreign nationals, the region expressed empathy, offering full understanding and care. In addition to regular authoritative updates and diplomatic notifications, a 24-hour hotline was set up and has received hundreds of calls, with staff diligently verifying and feeding back information. Currently, efforts are focused on rescue and recovery. After the search operation concludes, authorities will confirm and notify the status of deceased foreign nationals and assist families with follow-up procedures. For those still missing, assistance will be provided within China's legal framework, including arrangements for families visiting Xizang, in coordination with relevant foreign diplomatic missions, she added. Visiting the mudslide-hit area at Gyirong Port in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region on Sunday, two foreign journalists were impressed by China's response to the disaster and urged the international community to work together in tackling climate change. Reporters: Wang Xiaoyu, Palden Nyima and Shu Yiheng Video editor: Song Yi Editor: Liu Ming GYIRONG, Xizang -- China has provided assistance to 1,720 Nepalese border residents after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region on Aug 26, the emergency response and rescue headquarters said on Sunday. The mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, had left 43 people dead and 519 others missing at the border port as of 6 pm Saturday, officials told a news conference. Many Nepalese border residents who work or do business in the county of Gyirong were stranded there after the mudslide destroyed the border port, through which they enter and leave China. After a devastating mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region on Aug 26, 27-year-old Hao Zhen and 16 other volunteers from the "Go West" program joined the relief effort. Working behind the scenes in Gyirong town, the volunteers arranged accommodation, distributed supplies and helped provide meals for displaced residents and rescue workers. Hao said his comrades and himself were committed to playing their part wherever the motherland and the people needed them. As of 6 pm Saturday, more than 2,500 people and over 500 vehicles had been deployed to join rescue operations, and more than 1,000 flights of drones had air-dropped 5.43 metric tons of supplies, officials said. A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries have been identified as being among the missing, officials told a press conference attended by domestic and foreign journalists. The press conference was held after journalists from overseas media outlets visited the mudslide site at Gyirong Port over the weekend. China launched a massive search and rescue operation after the deadly mudslide, which was triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal. As of 6 pm Saturday, China has deployed more than 2,500 people and over 500 vehicles to join rescue operations. Drones have conducted more than 1,000 flights, and 5.43 tonnes of supplies have been air-dropped. Local authorities have provided assistance to 1,720 Nepalese border residents in Gyirong. Many Nepalese nationals who work or do business in Gyirong were stranded there after the mudslide destroyed the border port, through which they normally enter and leave China. China has also provided Nepal with daily updates on meteorological, hydrological and glacier data through a disaster information notification mechanism, according to officials. Until last month, Hao Zhen had only seen disaster relief efforts on the news. Then a devastating mudslide struck Gyirong, the remote border county in Xizang autonomous region where he works as a volunteer. While professional rescue teams searched the hardest-hit areas, Hao and his fellow volunteers worked behind the scenes, arranging accommodation, distributing supplies and helping provide meals for displaced residents and rescue workers. "When the disaster first happened, a lot of affected residents and rescuers arrived in the township all at once," Hao said. As relief supplies poured in, the volunteers counted, sorted and moved thousands of boxes donated by Red Cross organizations, companies and foundations. They also helped with logistical work at the local emergency response headquarters and collected and organized information from the disaster area. The experience gave Hao a new understanding of what disaster relief involves. Born in 1999, Hao is the oldest of the 17 Go West program volunteers working in Gyirong township. Most of the others were born between 2000 and 2003. They come from across China, including Heilongjiang, Jiangxi and Shandong provinces, as well as Xizang, and have backgrounds ranging from medicine to education. The work has come with practical challenges. Only two of the 17 volunteers speak Tibetan, creating communication difficulties at the shelters. Local township officials often stepped in to interpret. Food and accommodation were also stretched in the first few days as large numbers of residents, rescuers and support workers arrived in the small border town. Hao said the situation gradually improved as local authorities coordinated with hotels and restaurants to provide additional support. Another five Go West program volunteers remained in the county seat, helping receive relatives of missing people, assisting families and handling calls and follow-ups through the 12345 public service hotline. Volunteers from nearby counties, including Lhaze and Dingri, also came to help. For Hao, Gyirong is a long way from home — nearly 5,700 kilometers from Shuangyashan in Heilongjiang province. He usually makes the journey home only once a year. He arrived in Gyirong in February 2025 to join the Go West program and plans to stay for three years. His family initially tried to talk him out of the move, worried about the distance and the physical demands of living at high altitude. The physical challenges are real. When Hao first arrived in Gyirong, he found he did not have the same stamina he had at lower elevations. He also experienced heart palpitations when he first joined the relief effort. After more than a year on the plateau, however, he said his body has largely adapted. The Aug 26 mudslide at Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-altitude glacier in Nepal. As of Friday evening, 31 people had been confirmed dead and 531 remained missing in Gyirong, according to the local emergency response and rescue command headquarters. For Hao, the experience has also changed the way he sees the small tasks that fill much of his day. KATHMANDU -- Nepali rescuers on Saturday rescued a Chinese national from a hydropower plant hit by the deadly mudslide in Nepal, according to the Chinese Embassy in Nepal. The Chinese national was rescued by the Nepali Army in coordination with a disaster expert team from South Korea, 11 days after a devastating mudslide struck the area. The survivor was taken for further medical assessment and care. The rescue is part of an intensified effort to locate and evacuate people believed to be trapped inside hydropower project tunnels following a mudslide that swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems. The disaster caused extensive damage to several hydropower projects and other infrastructure in the affected areas. Some workers and other people are believed to have been trapped inside hydropower tunnels and have remained out of contact. Before the rescue of the Chinese national, the Nepali Army said in a social media post that a joint rescue team comprising 20 Nepali Army personnel and project representatives had been conducting search operations. The Nepali Army has been conducting search and rescue operations in coordination with foreign technical teams, including experts from China, India and South Korea, to reach people stranded inside structures at several hydropower projects. China has deployed around 20 sets of monitoring equipment across the disaster-hit Gyirong area in the Xizang autonomous region, with real-time data showing geological conditions stabilizing, a senior geologist said. The devices — including debris flow monitors, slope radars and microseismic sensors — were installed by the China Geological Survey and other emergency response teams following last month's ice-rock avalanche that buried parts of the Gyirong border crossing, causing massive casualties on both sides of the border. Ge Daqing, deputy director of the China Aero Geophysical Survey and Remote Sensing Center for Natural Resources, said the equipment was positioned at key risk points across the disaster zone to monitor slope movement, debris flow channels and ground deformation in real time. Two additional slope radars were installed on Wednesday near the border crossing after rescue teams cleared access roads, he added. The devices are positioned to protect workers repairing roads and power lines by issuing early warnings if falling rocks or shallow landslides are detected on the slopes above. Data collected so far indicates the dynamic processes at the site have entered a relatively stable phase. "Overall, there have been no significant fluctuations or changes," Ge said, adding that the risk of a large-scale secondary disaster is currently assessed as low without external triggers. However, he cautioned that high-risk factors persist due to the complex terrain. Some minor rockfalls have been observed at the glacier front in the collapse zone, but Ge said these pose no immediate threat. The monitoring equipment is primarily intended for the emergency response phase. Once a comprehensive risk assessment is completed and no major threats remain, the devices may be withdrawn, he said. Beyond the immediate response, the disaster has underscored the limitations of existing monitoring technologies in the high-altitude, cloud-prone Himalayan region. Ge said optical satellite imagery — the most common remote sensing tool — is severely hampered by persistent cloud cover and fog in the area. Clear images can be obtained on only about 20 days a year, and most of the optical data received recently have been obscured by clouds. To address this, Ge called for the accelerated development of new synthetic aperture radar satellites, particularly an interferometric SAR satellite constellation that combines L-band, high-resolution, wide-swath capabilities, and both sun-synchronous and low-inclination orbits. This can overcome the challenge of monitoring rapid deformation in the high-elevation mountains and glaciers of the Himalayas. He also stressed the need to improve satellite revisit cycles and spatial resolution to enable more frequent and rapid monitoring. Unmanned aerial vehicles offer another monitoring option, but current drones struggle to operate above 7,000 meters and their sensors remain vulnerable to cloud interference. New radar-based sensors and improved high-altitude flight capabilities are needed, he added. Looking ahead, Ge warned that the risk of high-altitude ice-rock avalanches in the region is likely to increase. "The 2015 Nepal earthquake caused internal damage to these mountain masses," he said. "Combined with glacial erosion at high elevations and steep terrain, the structural integrity of rock formations has been compromised, making them prone to collapse." Given the transboundary nature of such hazards, Ge highlighted the importance of international collaboration in disaster monitoring and early warning across the Himalayan region, noting that ice-rock avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods do not respect national borders. limenghan@chinadaily.com.cn The death toll from the massive mudslide that struck a border port in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, on Aug 26, rose to 31 as of 6 pm on Friday, while 531 people remained missing. A total of 987 personal items had also been recovered, according to the disaster emergency and rescue command headquarters. The rescue access route to Gyirong Port has been opened, marking a new stage in relief efforts, the headquarters said at a news conference on Friday evening. The command center said coordinated rescue operations would be further intensified, with particular emphasis on monitoring and early warning for secondary disasters at the port site and along the G216 highway. Local authorities will also continue to assess risks and issue early warnings for areas upstream and downstream of the disaster site to ensure the safety of rescue operations, the headquarters said. Since the mudslide hit Gyirong Port, an important land gateway between China and Nepal, round-the-clock rescue operations involving multiple government departments have been underway. As of 4 pm on Wednesday, 172 experts and technicians from meteorological, natural resources, water resources and emergency management departments, along with 150 sets of equipment, had been deployed to the site, according to the headquarters. The water resources authority, for example, sent 28 experts with 31 sets of equipment, including drones, radar water-level gauges and high-definition cameras, to conduct hydrological monitoring. The natural resources department dispatched 92 technicians with 40 sets of equipment to carry out focused surveys along two rescue access routes and in areas affected by the mudslide. The regional government has also moved swiftly to assess geological hazards in the disaster area. As of Wednesday, a special inspection along the G216 highway, a key rescue access route, had identified 58 geological hazard sites. Seven were classified as high-risk, 39 as medium-risk and 12 as low-risk, according to the headquarters. Local authorities have completed hazard inspections and risk assessments in three affected villages and identified two sites for temporary shelters, while providing guidance on their construction, the headquarters said. Technology has played a key role in the rescue operation. Slope radar, high-definition video surveillance and geophone monitoring systems have been installed in areas affected by ice-avalanche debris flows to continuously detect anomalies, including ice-rock collapses and deformation of debris in the source zone. By automatically collecting deformation and image data, the systems help address the limitations of manual inspections in the steep, canyon-locked terrain. They enable real-time monitoring of key hazard sites and help ensure the safety of rescue personnel working downstream, the command center said. In addition, local authorities have established a regular coordination mechanism to ensure smooth information flow throughout the rescue operation.

item.title: The commercial evolution of Yiwu
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
The commercial evolution of Yiwu Rise of China's small goods giant captured on celluloid Editor's note: With photographs captured through the decades, China Daily is presenting a series of visual chronicles to showcase how different fields evolved under the tide of China's reform and opening-up, and how that tide changed people's lives. In the early years of China's reform and opening-up, Yiwu, a small county-level city in Zhejiang province, was a resource-scarce land with a fragile economy. Its earliest pioneers shouldered wooden cases filled with candy, walking from village to village to trade sweets for chicken feathers. It was a humble, painstaking livelihood, barely enough to make ends meet. As the tide of the era shifted, so did Yiwu's fate. What began as a modest open-air street market at Huqingmen — where vendors laid out their wares on the bare ground — soon laid the groundwork for a burgeoning small-commodity trade market. From crude sheds and makeshift stalls, the market expanded through successive waves of modernization, ultimately evolving into the world-renowned Yiwu International Trade City. Over four decades, the market's architecture, trading methods and merchant community transformed beyond recognition — a process of continuous reinvention that continues to this day. This grassroots transformation — a county-level economic miracle — was systematically documented and preserved by local photographer Jin Fugen. For more than 40 years, his lens tracked the daily lives of countless ordinary merchants as they set up stalls, prepared goods, met buyers, negotiated orders, packed and shipped their goods. Through these micro-interactions, Jin captured the macro-narrative of Yiwu's rise from a local market to a global trade network. Decades of light and shadow live in his archives. Beyond preserving the hard work, adaptability and perseverance of generations of local entrepreneurs, these documentary photographs stand as a vivid record of China's broader private sector development, capturing a single city's journey into the global marketplace. Through the commercial evolution of one small city, they bear witness to the nation's opening-up and its embrace of the global market. From chicken feathers to world trade, from roadside stalls to the world's supermarket — Yiwu's trajectory is a story of building something from nothing and turning raw grit into economic momentum. In the quiet frames of Jin's photographs, that history remains strikingly dynamic.

item.title: Embrace of cultures still best lesson on understanding
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-08
Embrace of cultures still best lesson on understanding Renowned educator's return visit sheds light on positive results of exchanges When Ronald Sakolsky walked into a conference room in Beijing recently, he was immediately greeted by a former student he hadn't seen in 26 years. The embrace that followed — captured by cameras and shared across social media — became yet another symbol of the enduring power of people-to-people connections between China and the United States. Sakolsky, a retired history teacher from Pennsylvania, was in China for a 10-day visit from Aug 23 to Sept 1 at the invitation of the China Education Association for International Exchange. His journey — from Beijing to the Inner Mongolia autonomous region and Henan province — brought together the threads of a story that began in 1999, when he first came to Henan's Luoyang via a teacher exchange program that would ultimately transform hundreds of lives on both sides of the Pacific. The US-China Teachers Exchange Program operated from 1996 to 2014. It was run jointly by the China Education Association for International Exchange and the American Council of Learned Societies, which was later replaced by the National Committee on US-China Relations. During the 18 years, the program sent 332 Chinese teachers to schools across the US and brought 117 American teachers to Chinese classrooms. Margot Landman, former program director and deputy vice president of the NCUSCR, said what began as "a crazy idea, unclear in the details" grew into a bridge of understanding that continues to bear fruit long after the formal exchanges ended.
